## claude.ai Linear
When passing string values to tools, send the content directly without escape sequences. For example, use real newlines in markdown content rather than literal backslash-n (\n) characters.

## plugin:datadog:mcp
This is an MCP server for Datadog (a software observability platform). Consult Datadog docs if you're unsure about how something works in the platform. Docs for this MCP server can be found at https://docs.datadoghq.com/bits_ai/mcp_server/setup/ This server ships skill guides containing domain-specific guidance, workflows, and best practices that are not visible in tool names or schemas. Before invoking other tools, always perform skill discovery by running both paths in parallel: a direct load with `load_datadog_skill` using a general domain name (e.g. skill_name='datadog/traces'), and a call to `list_datadog_skills` with a fuzzy `query` based on topic keywords — load any clearly matching result from the listing along with the related skills it points to. The exception is a follow-up call in a domain whose skill you have already loaded or confirmed absent this session. If nothing clearly fits, do not load a skill — proceed with the tool descriptions. When the user asks to visualize, chart, or graph data — or when loading a data domain skill (e.g. datadog/traces, datadog/logs, datadog/metrics) — also load datadog/visualizations. Investigation results often benefit from charts.

Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines.   settings:
    gosec:
      excludes:
        - G204 # subprocess with variables is expected for git/opencode CLI wrappers
        - G702 # command injection via taint - controlled CLI inputs
        - G705 # XSS not applicable to CLI stderr output
    dupl:
      # Token threshold for duplication detection
      # Lower = more sensitive (catches smaller duplicates)
      # Default is 150. We use 75 for lint (blocks CI), `mise run dup` uses 50 (advisory)
      threshold: 75
    errcheck:
      check-type-assertions: true
      check-blank: true
    wrapcheck:
      # Errors from the generated control-plane client are mapped centrally
      # by renderCoreError (cmd/entire/cli/corecmd.go), which extracts the
      # RFC 7807 problem detail via errors.As. Per-call-site wrapping would
      # only be unwrapped again, so the command closures return coreapi
      # errors verbatim.
      #
      # checkpointpolicy.EnsureCanReadVersion already returns a clean,
      # user-facing message (including the checkpoint ID and version), and
      # callers classify it via IsUnsupportedVersion. Wrapping would obscure
      # that purpose-built message, so call sites return it verbatim.
      ignore-package-globs:
        - github.com/entireio/cli/internal/coreapi
        - github.com/entireio/cli/cmd/entire/cli/checkpointpolicy
    forbidigo:
      analyze-types: true
      forbid:
        - pattern: '^os\.Getwd$'
          msg: "os.Getwd() breaks when running from subdirectories - use paths.RepoRoot() for git-relative paths"
          pkg: '^os$'
        - pattern: '^.*\.Reset$'
          msg: "go-git Reset deletes .gitignored dirs - use HardResetWithProtection() from common.go"
          pkg: 'github\.com/go-git/go-git'
        - pattern: '^.*\.Checkout$'
          msg: "go-git Checkout deletes .gitignored dirs - use CheckoutBranch() from git_operations.go"
          pkg: 'github\.com/go-git/go-git'
        - pattern: '^.*Worktree\.Status$'
          msg: "go-git Worktree.Status() walks the whole worktree - use gitrepo.Status(ctx, repo)"
          pkg: 'github\.com/go-git/go-git'
        - pattern: '^.*\.(Print|Println|Printf)$'
          msg: "cobra's Print* writes to OutOrStderr (stderr in production); use fmt.Fprint*(cmd.OutOrStdout(), ...)"
          pkg: 'github\.com/spf13/cobra'
    govet:
      enable-all: true
      disable:
        - fieldalignment
        - shadow
    nolintlint:
      require-explanation: true
      require-specific: true
    sloglint:
      attr-only: true
    testifylint:
      enable-all: true
    unparam:
      check-exported: true
  exclusions:
    presets:
      - comments
      - std-error-handling
    rules:
      - path: _test\.go
        linters:
          - gosec
          - wrapcheck
          - forbidigo
      - path: ^e2e/
        linters:
          - errcheck
          - gochecknoinits
          - goconst
          - gosec
          - noctx
          - revive
          - usetesting
          - wrapcheck

      - path: ^cmd/entire/cli/integration_test/
        linters:
          - gosec

content.text:
## Root cause

`cmd /c start` was handing the OAuth URL to **cmd.exe, which treats an unquoted `&` as a command separator**. The URL was truncated at the first `&`.

`cmd/entire/cli/login.go:536` (as shipped in v0.10.0 — I confirmed via `git show v0.10.0`):

```go
case "windows":
    command = "cmd"
    args = []string{"/c", "start", "", browserURL}
```

Go's escaping doesn't save you here: `syscall.EscapeArg` only quotes an argument containing a space, tab, quote, or backslash. A URL has none of those, so it reaches cmd.exe bare.

The authorize URL is built with `url.Values.Encode()`, which sorts keys — so `client_id` comes first and `redirect_uri` sits behind three `&`s:

```
…/authorize?client_id=entire-cli&code_challenge=…&code_challenge_method=S256&redirect_uri=…
                                ^ cmd.exe cuts here
```

Leaving exactly `https://us.auth.entire.io/authorize?client_id=entire-cli` — byte-for-byte what your user reported, hence "missing redirect uri". Only the default browser flow is affected; `--device` isn't (see below).

It's macOS/Linux-only-tested code that's been broken since Mar 2026 (`5c44ffb87`), and only became user-visible when the browser redirect became the default login.

## Immediate workaround for the user

```
entire login --device
```

I verified against the live endpoint that its URL is `https://us.auth.entire.io/cli/auth?user_code=XXXX-XXXX` — a single query param, no `&`, so it survives cmd.exe intact. The device flow also prints the URL unconditionally, so copy-paste always works.

## Fix

Split the launcher per platform and, on Windows, call the Win32 `ShellExecute` API directly — no command line, so nothing to parse or escape. This is what `github.com/pkg/browser` switched to, and `golang.org/x/sys` was already a direct dependency.

- `cmd/entire/cli/browser_open_windows.go` (new) — `ShellExecute` via a `shellExecute` seam for testing
- `cmd/entire/cli/browser_open_other.go` (new) — `open`/`xdg-open`, unchanged behavior
- `cmd/entire/cli/login.go` — `openBrowser` keeps URL validation and the under-test guard, then delegates

Quoting alone wouldn't have been enough: the percent-encoded `redirect_uri` also exposes the URL to cmd's `%VAR%` expansion.

Tests: `browser_open_windows_test.go` asserts the whole URL reaches the shell association, plus a second test that executes `cmd /c echo <url>` to pin the truncation as the root cause so nobody reintroduces the shell. Both have `Windows` in the name, so the existing `test-windows` CI job (`-run '(Windows|MSYS)'`) picks them up. `browser_open_test.go` covers scheme validation cross-platform.

Verified: builds for darwin/windows/linux, `golangci-lint` clean on both darwin and `GOOS=windows` (the default run skips `_windows.go` files), and `mise run test:ci` passed. The Windows tests compile for windows/amd64 but I couldn't execute them here — they'll run on the CI Windows job.

## One thing worth deciding separately

`runBrowserLogin` (`login.go:289`) only prints the full URL when `openURL` returns an error. The truncated launch *succeeded* from our side, so the user got no copy-paste fallback — dead end. A successful browser spawn isn't proof the browser got a usable URL. I left that as-is since it's outside this bug, but printing the URL unconditionally (as the device flow does) would have made this self-service.

Changes are uncommitted — let me know if you want them on a branch/PR.

fix(login): open the browser via ShellExecute on Windows

`entire login` on Windows opened
https://us.auth.entire.io/authorize?client_id=entire-cli and the

as the root cause so the shell launcher is not reintroduced.

browser open reports failure, so this mangled-but-"successful" launch

gh pr create --base main --head soph/investigate-login-windows --title "fix(login): open the browser via ShellExecute on Windows" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## The bug

A user on Windows running v0.10.0 reported that `entire login` opens

```
https://us.auth.entire.io/authorize?client_id=entire-cli
```

and the authorization server rejects it with **"auth request is missing redirect uri"**.

## Root cause

`openBrowser` launched the URL through cmd.exe:

```go
case "windows":
    command = "cmd"
    args = []string{"/c", "start", "", browserURL}
```

cmd.exe treats an unquoted `&` as a command separator, so the browser only ever received the text before the first `&`.

Go's argv escaping does not help here: `syscall.EscapeArg` only quotes an argument containing a space, tab, quote, or backslash, and a URL has none of those, so it reaches cmd.exe bare. Because `url.Values.Encode` sorts keys, `client_id` sorts first and `redirect_uri` sits behind three separators:

```
…/authorize?client_id=entire-cli&code_challenge=…&code_challenge_method=S256&redirect_uri=…
                                ^ cmd.exe cuts here
```

which is byte-for-byte the URL in the report.

Quoting alone would not have been enough either — the percent-encoded `redirect_uri` also exposes the URL to cmd's `%VAR%` expansion.

Broken since 5c44ffb87 (Mar 2026), but only user-visible once the browser redirect became the default login flow.

## The fix

Split the launcher per platform and, on Windows, call the Win32 `ShellExecute` API directly (as `github.com/pkg/browser` does) so the URL is passed as a single wide string — no command line to parse, nothing to escape. `golang.org/x/sys` was already a direct dependency.

- `browser_open_windows.go` (new) — `ShellExecute`, behind a `shellExecute` var so tests can capture the string without launching a browser
- `browser_open_other.go` (new) — `open` / `xdg-open`, behavior unchanged; these never involved a shell
- `login.go` — `openBrowser` keeps URL validation and the under-test guard, then delegates to `openBrowserPlatform`

## Workaround for affected users, until this ships

```
entire login --device
```

Its `verification_uri_complete` carries a single query parameter (verified against the live endpoint), so it survives cmd.exe intact — and the device flow prints the URL unconditionally.

## Tests

Two Windows tests, named so the existing `test-windows` CI job picks them up (it selects `-run '(Windows|MSYS)'`):

- `TestOpenBrowserWindows_PassesWholeURLToShellAssociation` — the whole URL, `&` separators and percent-encoding intact, reaches the shell association
- `TestOpenBrowserWindows_CmdTruncatesURLAtFirstAmpersand` — executes `cmd /c echo <url>` to pin the truncation as the root cause, so the shell launcher is not reintroduced (`echo` stands in for `start`, so nothing launches)

Plus `browser_open_test.go` covering scheme validation cross-platform.

Verified: builds for darwin/windows/linux; `golangci-lint` clean on both darwin and `GOOS=windows` (the default run skips `_windows.go` files); `mise run test:ci` passes. The Windows tests compile for windows/amd64 but were not executed locally — they run in CI.

## Deliberately not addressed

`runBrowserLogin` only prints the full URL when the browser open *reports failure*. This launch succeeded from our side while delivering a mangled URL, so the user had no copy-paste fallback and was fully stuck. Printing the URL unconditionally (as the device flow does) would make this self-service, but that is a separate behavior change.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)
EOF
)" 2>&1 | tail -5

`/simplify → 4 cleanup agents in parallel → apply the fixes`

You are improving the quality of the changed code, not hunting for bugs. Review
it for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude issues, then fix what you
find. Do not look for correctness bugs — that is what `/code-review` is for.

## Phase 0 — Gather the diff

Run `git diff @{upstream}...HEAD` (or `git diff main...HEAD` / `git diff HEAD~1`
if there's no upstream) to get the unified diff under review. If there are
uncommitted changes, or the range diff is empty, also run `git diff HEAD` and
include the working-tree changes in scope — the review often runs before the
commit. If a PR number, branch name, or file path was passed as an argument,
review that target instead. Treat this diff as the review scope.

## Phase 1 — Review (4 cleanup agents in parallel)

Launch **4 independent review agents** via the Agent tool, all in a
single message so they run concurrently. Pass each agent the diff and one of
the four angles below. Each returns its findings with `file`, `line`, a
one-line `summary`, and the concrete cost (what is duplicated, wasted, or
harder to maintain).

### Reuse

Flag new code that re-implements something the codebase
already has — Grep shared/utility modules and files adjacent to the change,
and name the existing helper to call instead.

### Simplification

Flag unnecessary complexity the diff adds: redundant or derivable state,
copy-paste with slight variation, deep nesting, dead code left behind. Name
the simpler form that does the same job.

### Efficiency

Flag wasted work the diff introduces: redundant computation or repeated I/O,
independent operations run sequentially, blocking work added to startup or
hot paths. Also flag long-lived objects built from closures or captured
environments — they keep the entire enclosing scope alive for the object's
lifetime (a memory leak when that scope holds large values); prefer a
class/struct that copies only the fields it needs. Name the cheaper
alternative.

### Altitude

Check that each change is implemented at the right depth, not as a fragile
bandaid. Special cases layered on shared infrastructure are a sign the fix
isn't deep enough — prefer generalizing the underlying mechanism over adding
special cases.

## Phase 2 — Apply the fixes

Wait for all four agents to complete, dedup findings that point at the same
line or mechanism, and fix each remaining one directly. Skip any finding whose
fix would change intended behavior, require changes well outside the reviewed
diff, or that you judge to be a false positive — note the skip rather than
arguing with it. Finish with a brief summary of what was fixed and what was
skipped (or confirm the code was already clean).

+package cli
+
+import (
+	"context"
+	"fmt"
+
+	"golang.org/x/sys/windows"
+)
+
+// shellExecute is the Win32 entry point openBrowserPlatform launches through.
+// It is a variable so the Windows test can capture the exact string handed to
+// the shell association without launching a real browser.
+var shellExecute = windows.ShellExecute
+
+// openBrowserPlatform hands browserURL to the Windows shell association for
+// its scheme, which is the user's default browser.
+//
+// This calls ShellExecute rather than spawning `cmd /c start` on purpose. An
+// OAuth authorization URL carries `&` between query parameters and `%XX`
+// inside the percent-encoded redirect_uri, and both are cmd.exe
+// metacharacters: `&` ends the command, `%VAR%` expands. Go's argv escaping
+// does not help, because syscall.EscapeArg only quotes arguments containing a
+// space, tab, quote, or backslash — a URL has none of those, so it reached
+// cmd.exe bare and the browser only ever saw the text before the first `&`.
+// ShellExecute takes the URL as a single wide string, so there is no command
+// line to parse and no escaping to get wrong.
+//
+// hwnd is 0 (no owner window — this is a console app) and the verb is nil so
+// the association's default verb ("open") applies. ShellExecute returns once
+// the browser has been asked to open the URL; there is no child process for us
+// to wait on or release.
+func openBrowserPlatform(_ context.Context, browserURL string) error {
+	if err := shellExecute(0, nil, windows.StringToUTF16Ptr(browserURL), nil, nil, windows.SW_SHOWNORMAL); err != nil {
+		return fmt.Errorf("open browser via ShellExecute: %w", err)
+	}
+	return nil
+}

+// (`&`) and percent-encoding in the URL are passed through literally — see
+// browser_open_windows.go for what happens when a shell does get involved.
+func openBrowserPlatform(ctx context.Context, browserURL string) error {
+	var command string

+	case darwinGOOS:

+	case "linux":

+package cli
+
+import (
+	"context"
+	"fmt"
+
+	"golang.org/x/sys/windows"
+)
+
+// shellExecute is the Win32 entry point openBrowserPlatform launches through.
+// It is a variable so the Windows test can capture the exact string handed to
+// the shell association without launching a real browser.
+var shellExecute = windows.ShellExecute
+
+// openBrowserPlatform hands browserURL to the Windows shell association for
+// its scheme, which is the user's default browser.
+//
+// This calls ShellExecute rather than spawning `cmd /c start` on purpose. An
+// OAuth authorization URL carries `&` between query parameters and `%XX`
+// inside the percent-encoded redirect_uri, and both are cmd.exe
+// metacharacters: `&` ends the command, `%VAR%` expands. Go's argv escaping
+// does not help, because syscall.EscapeArg only quotes arguments containing a
+// space, tab, quote, or backslash — a URL has none of those, so it reached
+// cmd.exe bare and the browser only ever saw the text before the first `&`.
+// ShellExecute takes the URL as a single wide string, so there is no command
+// line to parse and no escaping to get wrong.
+//
+// hwnd is 0 (no owner window — this is a console app) and the verb is nil so
+// the association's default verb ("open") applies. ShellExecute returns once
+// the browser has been asked to open the URL; there is no child process for us
+// to wait on or release.
+func openBrowserPlatform(_ context.Context, browserURL string) error {
+	if err := shellExecute(0, nil, windows.StringToUTF16Ptr(browserURL), nil, nil, windows.SW_SHOWNORMAL); err != nil {
+		return fmt.Errorf("open browser via ShellExecute: %w", err)
+	}
+	return nil
+}

+package cli

+import (

+)
+
+// authorizeURLWithSeparators is shaped like a real authorization URL: url.Values
+// sorts its keys, so client_id comes first and redirect_uri sits behind three
+// `&` separators, and the redirect_uri itself is percent-encoded.
+const authorizeURLWithSeparators = "https://us.auth.entire.io/authorize?" +
+	"client_id=entire-cli&code_challenge=Zt1c&code_challenge_method=S256&" +
+	"redirect_uri=http%3A%2F%2F127.0.0.1%3A54123%2Fcallback&response_type=code&" +
+	"scope=cli+offline_access&state=Yg8q"
+
+// TestOpenBrowserWindows_PassesWholeURLToShellAssociation is the regression
+// test for a Windows `entire login` that opened
+// https://us.auth.entire.io/authorize?client_id=entire-cli and was rejected
+// with "auth request is missing redirect uri". The whole URL — every `&`
+// separator and the percent-encoded redirect_uri — must reach the browser.
+func TestOpenBrowserWindows_PassesWholeURLToShellAssociation(t *testing.T) {
+	// No t.Parallel(): this swaps the package-level shellExecute seam.
+	var got string
+	original := shellExecute
+	shellExecute = func(_ windows.Handle, _, file, _, _ *uint16, _ int32) error {
+		got = windows.UTF16PtrToString(file)
+		return nil
+	}
+	t.Cleanup(func() { shellExecute = original })
+
+	if err := openBrowserPlatform(t.Context(), authorizeURLWithSeparators); err != nil {
+		t.Fatalf("openBrowserPlatform: %v", err)
+	}
+
+	if got != authorizeURLWithSeparators {
+		t.Errorf("URL handed to the shell association was mangled:\n got: %s\nwant: %s", got, authorizeURLWithSeparators)
+	}
+}
+
+// TestOpenBrowserWindows_CmdTruncatesURLAtFirstAmpersand pins the root cause,
+// so nobody reintroduces `cmd /c start "" <url>` as the launcher. cmd.exe
+// treats an unquoted `&` as a command separator, and Go cannot help here:
+// syscall.EscapeArg only quotes an argument containing a space, tab, quote, or
+// backslash, and a URL has none of those, so it reaches cmd.exe bare. `echo`
+// stands in for `start` so the test observes the truncation without launching
+// anything.
+func TestOpenBrowserWindows_CmdTruncatesURLAtFirstAmpersand(t *testing.T) {
+	t.Parallel()
+
+	// Stdout only: cmd also tries to run each `&`-separated remainder as a
+	// command, and those failures land on stderr.
+	out, _ := exec.CommandContext(t.Context(), "cmd", "/c", "echo", authorizeURLWithSeparators).Output() //nolint:errcheck // nonzero exit is expected; the truncated stdout is the observation
+	echoed := strings.TrimSpace(string(out))
+
+	// Exactly the URL the bug report showed: everything from code_challenge
+	// onwards, redirect_uri included, was lost.
+	const truncated = "https://us.auth.entire.io/authorize?client_id=entire-cli"
+	if echoed != truncated {
+		t.Fatalf("expected cmd.exe to truncate at the first ampersand\n got: %s\nwant: %s", echoed, truncated)
+	}
+}

## Verdict: right depth for its bug class — there is no second instance. The altitude gap is in what stops the *next* one.

### 1. KEY QUESTION — no other unfixed instances (verified exhaustively, negative result)

Only three non-test sites in the repo hand a string to a Windows shell. Two are not this bug class, by construction:

**`cmd/entire/cli/versioncheck/autoupdate.go:133`** — `exec.CommandContext(ctx, "cmd", "/C", cmdStr)`. Not the same class. `cmdStr` comes from `updateCommand()` (`versioncheck.go:394`), which returns only compile-time constants, and `canAutoInstall()` (`versioncheck.go:377`) gates Windows to `scoop update entire/cli` / `mise upgrade entire`. The one string with a metacharacter (`curl … | bash`) can only reach the `sh -c` branch, where the pipe is *wanted*. No dynamic value, no `&`, no `%`.

**`cmd/entire/cli/agent/hook_command.go:137,158,168,293`** — the cmd.exe hook wrappers. The `command` interpolated into `(%s)` is built entirely from compile-time constants: `"entire hooks codex "` + a const hook name (`codex/hooks.go:80-93`, `cursor/hooks.go:118-131`). The one variant carrying a dynamic value — `LocalDevHookScript` with its `$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)` — can never reach the Windows wrapper, because `UseWindowsProductionHooks` returns false when `localDev` (`hook_command.go:283`). The genuinely variable part, the JSON warning payload, goes through `escapeWindowsCMD`. Covered.

Also checked and cleared, since each looked like a candidate: `redact/opf.go:377` runs the **user-configurable** `OPFSettings.Command` as `exec.CommandContext(ctx, s.command, args...)` — bare binary, no shell. `cmd/entire/cli/mcp.go:218` `strings.Fields(call.Arguments.Command)` is resolved in-process against the Cobra tree, never exec'd. Git hooks are `#!/bin/sh` with `shellQuote` on the embedded exe path (`strategy/hooks.go:507`). The pager at `explain.go:3012` is `exec.CommandContext(ctx, pager)` — no shell.

**So the fix is not a bandaid — it is the whole population of the bug.** What it does not do is prevent the next one; the invariant is currently guarded by one behavioural test on one function.

### 2. Two philosophies — the split is coherent, but the boundary is stated nowhere

- `escapeWindowsCMD` (`agent/hook_command.go:235`) = **escape**, because Entire writes a string into *someone else's* config file (Cursor/Codex `hooks.json`) and a third party performs the exec. Bypassing the shell is not available there.
- `openBrowserPlatform` (`browser_open_windows.go:32`) = **avoid the shell**, because Entire performs the exec itself.

The dividing line — *who owns the exec* — is principled and correct. The problem is that neither doc comment mentions the other, and the two comments are already discussing the same hazard from opposite sides without acknowledging it: `hook_command.go:232` says "`%` is deliberately NOT escaped… if that changes, percent expansion needs separate handling," while the new `login.go:516` says percent-encoded URLs are exposed to `%VAR%` expansion "too, so quoting alone would not be enough." A reader who lands on `escapeWindowsCMD` first gets no signal that it must not be used to launch something.

**Recommendation (cheap, high value):** two reciprocal sentences. On `escapeWindowsCMD`: "Use this only when a third party owns the exec. When Entire launches something itself, do not escape — bypass the shell (see `browser_open_windows.go`)." And the converse pointer on `openBrowserPlatform`.

### 3. CLAUDE.md — yes, and there is a section shaped exactly for it

`CLAUDE.md`/`AGENTS.md` (symlink) contain **zero** mentions of `cmd.exe` and no Windows-exec guidance at all; `docs/` has none either. The natural home is a new `####` sibling under `## Code Patterns`, modeled on `#### Opening Repositories - Always Use gitrepo` (`CLAUDE.md:494`) and `#### Reading Worktree Status` (`:519`) — which have precisely this shape: the invariant, the non-obvious behaviours you don't get otherwise, "Reviewers should flag any new…", and Key files. Content: the who-owns-the-exec rule from §2, plus the fact that made this bug possible and currently lives only in a Go comment (`syscall.EscapeArg` quotes only on space/tab/quote/backslash, so a URL passes through bare).

**On enforcement, be honest about what's available.** `CLAUDE.md:519` cites a forbidigo rule as the teeth for the analogous `gitrepo.Status` invariant. Forbidigo **cannot** express this one — `analyze-types` matches call targets, not argument values, so it can't separate `exec.CommandContext(ctx, "cmd", …)` from the ~100 legitimate `…, "git", …` calls. The usable local precedent is `cmd/entire/cli/deprecated_strings_test.go`, a `filepath.WalkDir` source sweep that fails on forbidden literals in non-test `.go` files. A ~30-line sibling asserting that no production file outside `agent/hook_command.go` passes `"cmd"`/`"cmd.exe"` as argv[0] would pin this mechanically. That is the one thing genuinely missing at this altitude.

### 4. Per-platform file split — right, and forced rather than chosen

`windows.ShellExecute` comes from `golang.org/x/sys/windows`, which doesn't compile off Windows, so a single function with a `runtime.GOOS` switch is not an option. Not a style call. `_other.go` + `//go:build !windows` also has direct local precedent (`interactive/rawmode_other.go`, `proclive/proc_other.go`).

One consistency nit: **`browser_open_windows.go` carries no `//go:build windows` tag**, while all four existing production `_windows.go` files do — `execx/execx_windows.go`, `procutil/procutil_windows.go`, `internal/flock/flock_windows.go`, `checkpoint/remote/command_cancel_windows.go`. Functionally identical, but the new pair ends up asymmetric (the `!windows` side tagged, the windows side not) against 4/4 precedent. One line. (No tag on the *test* file is fine — `agent/hook_command_exec_windows_test.go` has none either.)

Minor: the `!windows` file keeps a `runtime.GOOS` switch over darwin/linux and errors for e.g. freebsd, whereas the closest analogue `interactive/rawmode_*` splits all the way. Not worth changing for `open` vs `xdg-open`; noting only that the split is a hybrid rather than following the three-file precedent.

### 5. Blast radius — correct, and it silently fixes a second user-visible bug

`openBrowser` has exactly two production callers, both fixed: `login.go:97` (covering both the browser and `--device` flows, since `runLogin` at `login.go:158` receives the same func) and `experts_tui.go:233` via `openExpertsSessionCmd`. The second one matters — `primarySessionURL` (`experts_tui.go:218`) builds `expertsSessionURL(repo, sessionID)`, so **"open session" in `entire experts --tui` was silently broken on Windows by the same truncation**, and this change fixes it. Worth stating in the commit/PR, which currently only claims `login`.

There is exactly one browser-open path in the repo: a literal search for `ShellExecute`/`rundll32`/`explorer.exe`/`xdg-open`/`start ""` across all Go files returns only the new files plus `login.go`; `internal/` and `redact/` contain no browser code; `go.mod` pulls in no `pkg/browser`-style dependency. Nothing was left on a shell.

### Recommended actions, in priority order

1. Add the source-sweep test pinning "no production file outside `agent/hook_command.go` passes `cmd`/`cmd.exe` as argv[0]", following `deprecated_strings_test.go`.
2. Add the `#### Windows…` invariant to `CLAUDE.md` under `## Code Patterns`, in the `gitrepo` sections' shape.
3. Add the two reciprocal doc sentences between `escapeWindowsCMD` and `openBrowserPlatform` naming the who-owns-the-exec boundary.
4. Mention the `experts --tui` fix in the PR description.
5. Add `//go:build windows` to `browser_open_windows.go`.</result>

Measured: 20 opens → 21 goroutines, still 21 after `cancel()` + `runtime.GC()`.

goroutines before: 1
goroutines after 20 opens (ctx live): 21
goroutines after ctx cancel + GC: 21

#### Invoking Commands on Windows - Never Put a Dynamic Value on a cmd.exe Line

**When Entire performs the exec itself, do not go through `cmd.exe`.** Pass the
program and its arguments as separate argv elements (`exec.Command(prog, arg)`),
or call the Win32 API directly.

cmd.exe treats `&`, `|`, `<`, `>` as command separators/redirections and expands
`%VAR%`, and **Go's argv escaping will not protect you**: `syscall.EscapeArg`
only quotes an argument containing a space, tab, quote, or backslash. A URL,
a percent-encoded path, or any `&`-bearing string therefore reaches cmd.exe bare
and is silently cut at the first metacharacter. That is exactly how
`entire login` shipped a Windows build that opened
`…/authorize?client_id=entire-cli` and got rejected for a missing
`redirect_uri` — the `cmd /c start "" <url>` launcher lost everything from the
first `&` on, and because the truncation happened inside the released child, the
CLI saw a successful launch and printed no fallback URL.

Escaping is the right tool in exactly one situation: **a third party owns the
exec.** When Entire writes a command into an agent's config file (Cursor/Codex
`hooks.json`) and that agent runs it through cmd.exe, there is no shell to
avoid — use `agent.escapeWindowsCMD`. Reviewers should flag any new
`exec.Command("cmd", …)` / `"cmd.exe"` call site that interpolates a
non-constant value.

Key files: `cmd/entire/cli/browser_open_windows.go` (ShellExecute, the
avoid-the-shell side) and `cmd/entire/cli/agent/hook_command.go`
(`escapeWindowsCMD`, the third-party-exec side). Each doc comment points at the
other.

content.text:
Pushed to PR #1981 as `85e88ba47`. Four reviews ran; here's what changed.

## Fixed

**Deleted the cmd.exe truncation test** — flagged independently by two agents, and they were right in a way I'd missed: it called no code from this repo, so it passed identically whether the launcher used `ShellExecute` or `cmd /c start`. It could not detect the regression its own comment claimed to guard. The sibling seam test is the actual guard. It was also spawning a cmd.exe process plus six failed PATH×PATHEXT resolutions (one per `&`) on every Windows CI run to assert a third party's behavior.

**A goroutine leak I'd carried over verbatim** from the old launcher — the one genuinely new defect found. `exec.CommandContext` sets `Cmd.Cancel`, so `Start` spawns a `watchCtx` goroutine whose result channel only `Wait` drains, and this path deliberately never calls `Wait`. I measured it: 20 opens leaked 20 goroutines, surviving cancel *and* GC; with `exec.Command`, zero. The context was already inert because `Process.Release` detaches the child, so `Cmd.Cancel`'s `Process.Kill` fails regardless — dropping it loses no cancellation that ever worked. Bounded for `login`, but `experts --tui` is long-lived and opens several links.

**Consolidated the rationale** — the `&`/`EscapeArg`/`%VAR%` explanation was in four files; now in one, on the function a future reader edits if tempted by `cmd /c start`. Shared one authorize-URL fixture across both test files, folded two cross-platform tests into a table, added the `//go:build windows` tag (4/4 existing production `_windows.go` files carry it).

**Named the boundary between the repo's two Windows philosophies.** `escapeWindowsCMD` and the new launcher were discussing the same hazard from opposite sides without referencing each other. The split is principled — *who owns the exec*: escape when a third party runs your command (agents' `hooks.json`), bypass the shell when Entire launches it. Reciprocal doc pointers plus a CLAUDE.md section under Code Patterns.

## Skipped

**One claim was wrong.** The altitude agent reported `experts --tui` was also silently broken on Windows and wanted it in the PR. I checked `expertsSessionURL` — it builds a path-only URL via `url.PathEscape`, no query string, so no `&` and no truncation. Not added.

- **Source-sweep test banning `cmd` as argv[0]** — the real invariant is "no *dynamic* value on a cmd line," which a literal sweep can't express. It would also flag the legitimate constant-only usage in `versioncheck/autoupdate.go:133`, so it needs an allowlist and is a crude proxy. The CLAUDE.md note plus a review instruction is the honest level of enforcement available.
- **Collapsing the `runtime.GOOS` switch** to make the BSDs work — a real simplification, but it widens platform support inside a login bugfix. Left as-is, preserving pre-existing behavior.
- **Generalizing `execx.SpawnDetached`** to route the browser launch through it — it hardcodes `os.Executable()`, so this is well outside the diff.
- **Renaming to `_unix.go`** — I checked; `interactive/rawmode_other.go` uses exactly `_other.go` + a negated tag, so the naming already matches local precedent.

The four agents also confirmed, with measurements, that there is **no second instance of this bug class** in the repo (the other two cmd.exe call sites interpolate only compile-time constants), and that `x/sys/windows` was already in the Windows import graph — the fix costs +1,024 bytes of PE page rounding.

content.text:
Yes — and I verified both against the production auth server rather than reasoning about them.

## Forward this: `entire login --device`

```
entire login --device
```

Real output, captured from a run just now:

```
Device code: BN5V-FV8V
Login URL:   https://us.auth.entire.io/cli/auth?user_code=BN5V-FV8V

Waiting for approval...
```

Two reasons it's immune to the bug:

1. **One query parameter, no `&`** — there is nothing for cmd.exe to cut, so the browser gets the whole URL.
2. **The URL is printed unconditionally**, before any browser launch. Even if the open misbehaves, they copy-paste and it works. The browser flow only prints the URL when the open *reports* failure — which is precisely why they hit a dead end.

Approval then polls over HTTPS with no shell involved. This gets them fully logged in; nothing is degraded versus the redirect flow.

## Incidental confirmation of the diagnosis

Forcing the browser flow to print its URL produced this:

```
…/authorize?client_id=entire-cli&code_challenge=UwBw-uNt…&code_challenge_method=S256&redirect_uri=http%3A%2F%2F127.0.0.1%3A59656%2Fcallback&response_type=code&scope=cli+offline_access&state=moEAbe7a…
```

Cut at the first `&`, that is `https://us.auth.entire.io/authorize?client_id=entire-cli` — byte-for-byte what they reported. The diagnosis is now confirmed against a real authorize URL, not just inferred from the code.

## A second option, with a caveat

`ENTIRE_TEST_TTY=1 entire login` makes the browser open "fail" deliberately, so the CLI prints the full authorize URL and keeps the loopback listener waiting — paste it into a browser and the login completes on the redirect flow. Verified working (that's how I captured the URL above).

I'd hold this in reserve rather than lead with it: `ENTIRE_TEST_TTY` is an internal test switch, not a supported user-facing knob, and it also suppresses the Enter prompt as a side effect. Only reach for it if they specifically need the redirect flow.

## Getting the actual fix to them

PR #1981 isn't merged, so the current nightlies don't have it either — `--device` is the answer until it lands. Once merged, a nightly build carries it ahead of the next stable release.

1	<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
2	https://entire.io/gh/entireio/cli/trails/1037
3	<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->
4	
5	## The bug
6	
7	A user on Windows running v0.10.0 reported that `entire login` opens
8	
9	```
10	https://us.auth.entire.io/authorize?client_id=entire-cli
11	```
12	
13	and the authorization server rejects it with **"auth request is missing redirect uri"**.
14	
15	## Root cause
16	
17	`openBrowser` launched the URL through cmd.exe:
18	
19	```go
20	case "windows":
21	    command = "cmd"
22	    args = []string{"/c", "start", "", browserURL}
23	```
24	
25	cmd.exe treats an unquoted `&` as a command separator, so the browser only ever received the text before the first `&`.
26	
27	Go's argv escaping does not help here: `syscall.EscapeArg` only quotes an argument containing a space, tab, quote, or backslash, and a URL has none of those, so it reaches cmd.exe bare. Because `url.Values.Encode` sorts keys, `client_id` sorts first and `redirect_uri` sits behind three separators:
28	
29	```
30	…/authorize?client_id=entire-cli&code_challenge=…&code_challenge_method=S256&redirect_uri=…
31	                                ^ cmd.exe cuts here
32	```
33	
34	which is byte-for-byte the URL in the report.
35	
36	Quoting alone would not have been enough either — the percent-encoded `redirect_uri` also exposes the URL to cmd's `%VAR%` expansion.
37	
38	Broken since 5c44ffb87 (Mar 2026), but only user-visible once the browser redirect became the default login flow.
39	
40	## The fix
41	
42	Split the launcher per platform and, on Windows, call the Win32 `ShellExecute` API directly (as `github.com/pkg/browser` does) so the URL is passed as a single wide string — no command line to parse, nothing to escape. `golang.org/x/sys` was already a direct dependency.
43	
44	- `browser_open_windows.go` (new) — `ShellExecute`, behind a `shellExecute` var so tests can capture the string without launching a browser
45	- `browser_open_other.go` (new) — `open` / `xdg-open`, behavior unchanged; these never involved a shell
46	- `login.go` — `openBrowser` keeps URL validation and the under-test guard, then delegates to `openBrowserPlatform`
47	
48	## Workaround for affected users, until this ships
49	
50	```
51	entire login --device
52	```
53	
54	Its `verification_uri_complete` carries a single query parameter (verified against the live endpoint), so it survives cmd.exe intact — and the device flow prints the URL unconditionally.
55	
56	## Tests
57	
58	Two Windows tests, named so the existing `test-windows` CI job picks them up (it selects `-run '(Windows|MSYS)'`):
59	
60	- `TestOpenBrowserWindows_PassesWholeURLToShellAssociation` — the whole URL, `&` separators and percent-encoding intact, reaches the shell association
61	- `TestOpenBrowserWindows_CmdTruncatesURLAtFirstAmpersand` — executes `cmd /c echo <url>` to pin the truncation as the root cause, so the shell launcher is not reintroduced (`echo` stands in for `start`, so nothing launches)
62	
63	Plus `browser_open_test.go` covering scheme validation cross-platform.
64	
65	Verified: builds for darwin/windows/linux; `golangci-lint` clean on both darwin and `GOOS=windows` (the default run skips `_windows.go` files); `mise run test:ci` passes. The Windows tests compile for windows/amd64 but were not executed locally — they run in CI.
66	
67	## Deliberately not addressed
68	
69	`runBrowserLogin` only prints the full URL when the browser open *reports failure*. This launch succeeded from our side while delivering a mangled URL, so the user had no copy-paste fallback and was fully stuck. Printing the URL unconditionally (as the device flow does) would make this self-service, but that is a separate behavior change.

<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/entireio/cli/trails/1037
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

## The bug

A user on Windows running v0.10.0 reported that `entire login` opens

```
https://us.auth.entire.io/authorize?client_id=entire-cli
```

and the authorization server rejects it with **"auth request is missing redirect uri"**.

## Root cause

`openBrowser` launched the URL through cmd.exe:

```go
case "windows":
    command = "cmd"
    args = []string{"/c", "start", "", browserURL}
```

cmd.exe treats an unquoted `&` as a command separator, so the browser only ever received the text before the first `&`.

Go's argv escaping does not help here: `syscall.EscapeArg` only quotes an argument containing a space, tab, quote, or backslash, and a URL has none of those, so it reaches cmd.exe bare. Because `url.Values.Encode` sorts keys, `client_id` sorts first and `redirect_uri` sits behind three separators:

```
…/authorize?client_id=entire-cli&code_challenge=…&code_challenge_method=S256&redirect_uri=…
                                ^ cmd.exe cuts here
```

which is byte-for-byte the URL in the report.

Quoting alone would not have been enough either — the percent-encoded `redirect_uri` also exposes the URL to cmd's `%VAR%` expansion.

Broken since 5c44ffb87 (Mar 2026), but only user-visible once the browser redirect became the default login flow.

## The fix

Split the launcher per platform and, on Windows, call the Win32 `ShellExecute` API directly (as `github.com/pkg/browser` does) so the URL is passed as a single wide string — no command line to parse, nothing to escape. `golang.org/x/sys` was already a direct dependency.

- `browser_open_windows.go` (new) — `ShellExecute`, behind a `shellExecute` var so tests can capture the string without launching a browser
- `browser_open_other.go` (new) — `open` / `xdg-open`, behavior unchanged; these never involved a shell
- `login.go` — `openBrowser` keeps URL validation and the under-test guard, then delegates to `openBrowserPlatform`

## Workaround for affected users, until this ships

```
entire login --device
```

Its `verification_uri_complete` carries a single query parameter (verified against the live endpoint), so it survives cmd.exe intact — and the device flow prints the URL unconditionally.

## Tests

Two Windows tests, named so the existing `test-windows` CI job picks them up (it selects `-run '(Windows|MSYS)'`):

- `TestOpenBrowserWindows_PassesWholeURLToShellAssociation` — the whole URL, `&` separators and percent-encoding intact, reaches the shell association
- `TestOpenBrowserWindows_CmdTruncatesURLAtFirstAmpersand` — executes `cmd /c echo <url>` to pin the truncation as the root cause, so the shell launcher is not reintroduced (`echo` stands in for `start`, so nothing launches)

Plus `browser_open_test.go` covering scheme validation cross-platform.

Verified: builds for darwin/windows/linux; `golangci-lint` clean on both darwin and `GOOS=windows` (the default run skips `_windows.go` files); `mise run test:ci` passes. The Windows tests compile for windows/amd64 but were not executed locally — they run in CI.

## Deliberately not addressed

`runBrowserLogin` only prints the full URL when the browser open *reports failure*. This launch succeeded from our side while delivering a mangled URL, so the user had no copy-paste fallback and was fully stuck. Printing the URL unconditionally (as the device flow does) would make this self-service, but that is a separate behavior change.

## The bug

A user on Windows running v0.10.0 reported that `entire login` opens

```
https://us.auth.entire.io/authorize?client_id=entire-cli
```

and the authorization server rejects it with **"auth request is missing redirect uri"**.

## Root cause

`openBrowser` launched the URL through cmd.exe:

```go
case "windows":
    command = "cmd"
    args = []string{"/c", "start", "", browserURL}
```

cmd.exe treats an unquoted `&` as a command separator, so the browser only ever received the text before the first `&`.

Go's argv escaping does not help here: `syscall.EscapeArg` only quotes an argument containing a space, tab, quote, or backslash, and a URL has none of those, so it reaches cmd.exe bare. Because `url.Values.Encode` sorts keys, `client_id` sorts first and `redirect_uri` sits behind three separators.

Here is a real authorization URL from the production auth server:

```
…/authorize?client_id=entire-cli&code_challenge=UwBw-uNt…&code_challenge_method=S256&redirect_uri=http%3A%2F%2F127.0.0.1%3A59656%2Fcallback&response_type=code&scope=cli+offline_access&state=moEAbe7a…
                                ^ cmd.exe cuts here
```

Everything from `code_challenge` on is lost, leaving `…/authorize?client_id=entire-cli` — byte-for-byte the URL in the report.

Quoting alone would not have been enough either — the percent-encoded `redirect_uri` also exposes the URL to cmd's `%VAR%` expansion.

Broken since 5c44ffb87 (Mar 2026), but only user-visible once the browser redirect became the default login flow.

## Workaround for affected users, until this ships

```
entire login --device
```

Captured from a real run:

```
Device code: BN5V-FV8V
Login URL:   https://us.auth.entire.io/cli/auth?user_code=BN5V-FV8V

Waiting for approval...
```

Two reasons this is immune:

1. **One query parameter, no `&`** — there is nothing for cmd.exe to cut, so the browser receives the whole URL. Verified against the live `/device_authorization` endpoint.
2. **The URL is printed unconditionally**, before any browser launch, so copy-paste works even if the open misbehaves.

Approval then polls over HTTPS with no shell involved. Nothing is degraded relative to the redirect flow.

<details>
<summary>Second option, if the redirect flow is specifically needed</summary>

`ENTIRE_TEST_TTY=1 entire login` makes the browser open fail deliberately, so the CLI prints the full authorization URL and keeps the loopback listener waiting — paste it into a browser and the login completes on the redirect flow. (This is how the real URL above was captured.)

Hold this in reserve rather than recommending it: `ENTIRE_TEST_TTY` is an internal test switch, not a supported user-facing knob, and it also suppresses the Enter prompt as a side effect.

</details>

## The fix

Split the launcher per platform and, on Windows, call the Win32 `ShellExecute` API directly (as `github.com/pkg/browser` does) so the URL is passed as a single wide string — no command line to parse, nothing to escape. `golang.org/x/sys` was already a direct dependency, and already in the Windows import graph, so this costs +1,024 bytes of PE page rounding.

- `browser_open_windows.go` (new) — `ShellExecute`, behind a `shellExecute` var so tests can capture the string without launching a browser
- `browser_open_other.go` (new) — `open` / `xdg-open`; these never involved a shell
- `login.go` — `openBrowser` keeps URL validation and the under-test guard, then delegates to `openBrowserPlatform`

The second commit is a cleanup pass. Two things in it are worth calling out:

**A goroutine leak, carried over verbatim from the old launcher.** `exec.CommandContext` sets `Cmd.Cancel`, so `Start` spawns a `watchCtx` goroutine whose result channel only `Wait` drains — and this path deliberately never calls `Wait`. Every browser open leaked one goroutine, retaining the `Cmd` (argv, env, URL), for the process lifetime. Measured: 20 opens leaked 20 goroutines, surviving both cancel and GC; with `exec.Command` it is zero. The context was already inert here because `Process.Release` detaches the child, so `Cmd.Cancel`'s `Process.Kill` fails regardless — dropping it removes the leak without losing cancellation that ever worked. Bounded for `login`, but `experts --tui` is long-lived and opens several links.

**Naming the boundary between this repo's two Windows-command philosophies**, which previously discussed the same hazard from opposite sides without referencing each other. The split turns on *who owns the exec*: escape when a third party runs your command (`agent.escapeWindowsCMD`, for agents' `hooks.json`), bypass the shell when Entire launches it itself. Reciprocal doc pointers, plus a `CLAUDE.md` section under Code Patterns recording the invariant and the `EscapeArg` fact that made the bug possible.

## Tests

`TestOpenBrowserWindows_PassesWholeURLToShellAssociation`, named so the existing `test-windows` CI job picks it up (it selects `-run '(Windows|MSYS)'`): the whole URL, `&` separators and percent-encoding intact, reaches the shell association. Reintroducing a shell launcher stops the seam being called and fails this test.

Plus `browser_open_test.go` covering URL validation cross-platform.

An earlier revision also had a test asserting that `cmd /c echo <url>` truncates at the first `&`. It was dropped in the cleanup commit: it called no code from this repo, so it passed identically whether the launcher used `ShellExecute` or `cmd /c start`, and could not detect the regression it claimed to guard — while costing a cmd.exe process plus six failed PATH×PATHEXT resolutions on every Windows CI run.

Verified: builds for darwin/windows/linux; `golangci-lint` clean on both darwin and `GOOS=windows` (the default run skips `_windows.go` files); `mise run test:ci` passes. The Windows test compiles for windows/amd64 but was not executed locally — it runs in CI.

## Scope

`openBrowser` has two production callers and both are covered: `login.go` (browser and `--device` flows) and `experts_tui.go` via `openExpertsSessionCmd`. The experts session URL is path-only (`url.PathEscape`, no query string), so it had no `&` and was not affected by this bug — it just becomes robust for free.

This is the whole population of the bug class. The repo's only other cmd.exe call sites — `versioncheck/autoupdate.go` and the `agent/hook_command.go` wrappers — interpolate compile-time constants only, and the one genuinely variable value there already goes through `escapeWindowsCMD`.

## Deliberately not addressed

`runBrowserLogin` only prints the full URL when the browser open *reports failure*. This launch succeeded from our side while delivering a mangled URL, so the user had no copy-paste fallback and was fully stuck. Printing the URL unconditionally (as the device flow does) would make this class of failure self-service, but that is a separate behavior change.

content.text:
Your colleague is right, and it has an uncomfortable consequence for the PR. Let me correct the record.

## The mechanism

`interactive.go:55` — `CanPromptInteractively()` probes `/dev/tty`:

```go
tty, err := os.OpenFile("/dev/tty", os.O_RDWR, 0)
if err != nil {
    return false
}
```

Native Windows has no `/dev/tty`, so this always fails → `canPrompt: false` → `shouldUseBrowserLogin` (`!useDevice && canPrompt && !sshSession`) is false → device flow, always. The code even admits it, at `rawmode_other.go:9`: *"Those platforms don't have a /dev/tty for CanPromptInteractively to open either."*

"By design-ish" is generous though — this isn't scoped to login. **`CanPromptInteractively()` has 61 non-test call sites**, so on Windows every wizard, picker, confirm, and prompt in the CLI is off: `entire agent`'s selector, `session resume`'s picker, `repo clone`'s cluster prompt, the mirror wizard. Windows users get the non-interactive fallback everywhere. That looks like an unintended consequence of a POSIX-only probe, not a decision.

## What this does to my PR — I over-claimed

I need to correct something I stated confidently. On native Windows, `entire login` **never calls `openBrowser` at all**. The device flow's non-interactive branch (`login.go:186-188`) only prints the URL:

```go
} else {
    fmt.Fprintf(outW, "Login URL:   %s\n\n", approvalURL)
}
```

The only `openBrowser` path reachable on Windows is `entire experts --tui` (gated on `IsTerminalWriter`, which *does* work on Windows via `GetConsoleMode`) — and that URL is path-only with no `&`, so the old launcher handled it fine.

So the cmd.exe truncation I fixed was **not reachable with an `&`-bearing URL on native Windows**, and cannot be what your reporter hit. My claim that "this is how a Windows `entire login` opened `/authorize?client_id=entire-cli`" is not supportable. The launcher defect is real and the fix is correct — but it's latent hardening, not the reported bug.

## So where did their `/authorize` URL come from?

It requires the browser-redirect flow, which requires `/dev/tty`. Leading hypothesis: **they're in WSL, not native Windows.** That fits exactly — GOOS=linux, `/dev/tty` exists → browser flow → `/authorize?client_id=…&code_challenge=…`. We hand that to `xdg-open` as a single argv element, correctly. But in WSL `xdg-open` is usually a shim (`wslview`, or a hand-rolled script) that forwards to Windows via `cmd.exe /c start <url>` — commonly unquoted, which truncates at the first `&`.

If that's it, the truncation is in their shim and my fix doesn't touch it.

**Questions worth forwarding to the reporter:**

1. Did the CLI print `Device code: XXXX-XXXX` and `No interactive terminal detected; using device-code flow.`? If yes → native Windows, and the `/authorize` URL came from somewhere other than our launcher.
2. Or did it print `Logging in to: https://us.auth.entire.io` then `Press Enter to open in browser...`? If yes → browser flow → they have a `/dev/tty`, i.e. WSL.
3. If WSL: what does `cat $(which xdg-open)` / `readlink -f $(which xdg-open)` show?

## Two decisions for you

**The real bug is the TTY probe**, and it's the prerequisite that makes my launcher fix matter: fix Windows interactivity and the browser flow activates on Windows, at which point handing that URL to cmd.exe would truncate it. The fix is available — `x/term` ships `term_windows.go` using `GetConsoleMode`, and this repo already calls `term.IsTerminal` in `IsTerminalWriter`.

1. Want me to take on Windows TTY detection, or keep that separate from #1981?
2. The PR body and the second commit message both assert the bad causal claim. I can fix the body immediately; the commit message needs a force-push — say the word.

I haven't touched either yet, since how to reframe #1981 depends on the answers to the reporter's questions.

content.text:
Yes — substantially. It would mean my PR doesn't help them at all.

## What changes under WSL

**WSL builds are `GOOS=linux`.** `browser_open_windows.go` isn't compiled into their binary. They get `browser_open_other.go`:

```go
cmd := exec.Command("xdg-open", browserURL)
```

That's already correct — the URL is one argv element, no shell involved. There is nothing in our launcher to fix for them, before or after my PR.

**And `/dev/tty` exists in WSL**, so `canPrompt` is true → browser-redirect flow → an `/authorize?client_id=…&code_challenge=…` URL. That's the half your colleague's VM can't reproduce, and it matches the report exactly.

So both reports are true and neither is wrong: native Windows → device flow, no browser open; WSL → browser flow with the `/authorize` URL. Different platforms, different code paths.

**The truncation would then be inside their `xdg-open`.** Worth noting the shape this implies: a *bare* WSL without xdg-utils would actually work fine — `xdg-open` not found → `openBrowser` returns an error → `runBrowserLogin` prints the full URL and they copy-paste. The failure needs an `xdg-open` that resolves *and* forwards to Windows badly: `wslview`/`wslu`, or a `BROWSER` shim doing `cmd.exe /c start <url>` unquoted. Same cmd.exe defect as ours, one layer out, in code we don't own.

## Which promotes the thing I'd shelved

I'd listed "print the full URL unconditionally" under *deliberately not addressed*. Under the WSL hypothesis it becomes **the** fix, and I'd now argue it's more valuable than the ShellExecute change:

We can never control a third-party opener. What we control is whether a mangled launch is recoverable. Right now `runBrowserLogin` prints the URL only when the open *reports* failure, so any silently-mangling opener — ours before this PR, theirs today — produces a dead end. The device flow already prints it unconditionally; making the browser flow match is a few lines and fixes this class of failure regardless of whose launcher is at fault.

I'd skip WSL-specific detection. It's tempting to treat WSL like SSH and force the device flow, but WSL2's localhost forwarding usually makes the loopback redirect work, so that's a heavier fix than the problem needs. There's no WSL detection in the repo today.

## Three decisions, with my recommendation

1. **Print the URL unconditionally in the browser flow** — do this; it's the actual user-facing fix and platform-independent.
2. **Windows TTY detection** (`term.IsTerminal` instead of the `/dev/tty` probe) — the larger bug, 61 call sites, worth its own PR. Also what makes my ShellExecute fix load-bearing rather than latent.

content.text:
That screenshot overturns my last two answers. Let me correct them.

## Your reporter is on native Windows, and the browser flow ran

The output is unambiguously `runBrowserLogin`, not the device flow:

| Screenshot line | Source | Flow |
|---|---|---|
| `Logging in to: https://us.auth.entire.io/` | `login.go:280` | browser only |
| `Press Enter to open in browser...` | `login.go:281` | both |
| `Waiting for sign-in...` | `login.go:294` | **browser only** — device prints `Waiting for approval...` |

And there's no `Device code: XXXX-XXXX` / `Login URL:` pair, which the device flow always prints first. Combined with `OS/Arch: windows/amd64` and `PS C:\temp>`, that means `canPrompt` was **true** on native Windows and `shouldUseBrowserLogin` picked the browser flow.

So:

- **The WSL theory is dead.** Discard it.
- **My original diagnosis was right, and #1981 does fix their bug.** The `&`-bearing authorize URL was generated, handed to `cmd /c start`, and cut at the first `&`.
- `startBrowser(ctx)` clearly succeeded — no fallback warning — so the **loopback listener binds fine on Windows**. The browser flow is fully functional there *except* URL delivery, which is exactly what the PR fixes.
- The screenshot even shows the dead end I'd described: it sits at `Waiting for sign-in...` with no URL to copy, because the launch reported success.

Good thing I hadn't pushed that PR-body "correction" — the original claim was accurate and stays.

## What I got wrong, and the open question it leaves

I concluded from `interactive.go:55` that `os.OpenFile("/dev/tty", …)` cannot succeed on Windows, and told you the fix was latent hardening. The screenshot disproves that. I trusted a code reading over an actual observation.

I still can't explain the mechanism: Go has no `/dev/tty` special-casing on Windows (I checked `os`, `syscall`, `internal/syscall/windows` — only `DevNull = "NUL"`), and `/dev/tty` should resolve to `C:\dev\tty`. Yet empirically it returns a usable handle in a real PowerShell console.

That's worth nailing down rather than guessing, because it decides whether Windows login works dependably or by accident. The `test-windows` CI job gives us a clean way: a test that reports what that open actually does on a Windows runner.

## Reconciling with your colleague

Their claim and this screenshot can't both describe the same conditions. Either their VM run wasn't attached to a real interactive console the way a PowerShell session is (piped output, remote exec, or `CI` set would all flip `canPrompt` to false), or the claim came from reading the code — possibly reading my own analysis — rather than observing it. Worth asking which, since if it *was* observed, there's a second Windows variable we haven't found.

## Where that leaves the work

1. **#1981 stands as-is.** Correct fix, correct root cause, no body change needed.
2. **Print the URL unconditionally in the browser flow** — the screenshot is the argument for it. Their run had a working listener and a mangled URL and gave them nothing to fall back on. Still worth doing, now as hardening rather than as the fix.
3. **Resolve the `/dev/tty`-on-Windows question** via a Windows CI test before anyone makes claims about Windows interactivity in either direction.

Want me to add the unconditional URL print to #1981, and put up the Windows TTY probe test?

content.text:
Plausible in principle, but I don't think the shell is the variable — and I've already been wrong here once by trusting a code reading over an observation, so let me say what's testable rather than argue.

## Why cmd vs PowerShell shouldn't matter for this

The probe is `os.OpenFile("/dev/tty", os.O_RDWR, 0)` from a native Go binary — a `CreateFileW` call on a filesystem path. Both shells attach a console, set the same CWD, and resolve the same current drive, so path resolution is identical. Nothing in our code branches on the parent shell.

What *would* flip it between two runs: `CI` set in the environment, output piped or redirected rather than going to a console, or launching via WinRM/PsExec/SSH instead of an interactive session.

## A hypothesis that explains everything, including why your colleague disagrees

`/dev/tty` on Windows resolves drive-root-relative — to **`C:\dev\tty`**. If that path happens to exist on the reporter's machine, the probe opens it, `ttyInRawMode` returns false on Windows (`rawmode_other.go`), so `canPrompt` comes back **true** and they get the browser flow. A clean VM has no `C:\dev`, so the probe fails and your colleague gets the device flow.

That reconciles all three observations without needing a shell difference:

- Colleague, clean VM → device flow. Correct.
- Reporter, dev machine with a stray `C:\dev\tty` → browser flow → `&`-bearing authorize URL → cmd.exe truncation → their exact error. Correct.
- Same binary, same code, different outcome.

A `C:\dev` is the sort of thing POSIX-emulation tooling leaves behind, which fits someone with a heavily-tooled Windows box.

## One command settles it

Ask the reporter, in PowerShell:

```powershell
Test-Path C:\dev\tty; Test-Path C:\dev; $env:CI; $env:ENTIRE_TEST_TTY
```

If `C:\dev\tty` exists, the mystery is closed. And to test your hypothesis directly, have your colleague run `entire login` in both `cmd.exe` and PowerShell in the VM and report just the first line — `Logging in to:` means browser flow, `Device code:` means device flow.

## Either way, two things are already settled

The screenshot is proof that the browser flow **does** run on real native Windows and that the loopback listener binds there, so **#1981 is a real fix for a reachable bug** — that doesn't depend on how the probe succeeded.

And whichever way this lands, the probe is wrong on Windows: it either fails always (Windows never gets interactive prompts — 61 call sites) or succeeds by accident on machines with an unrelated file. It should be `term.IsTerminal` on the console handle, which `x/term` already implements for Windows and this repo already uses in `IsTerminalWriter`.

I can settle the probe question independently of both machines with a test on the `test-windows` CI job — it would tell us what that open actually does on a stock Windows runner. Want me to run that?

## The conflict

One file: `cmd/entire/cli/login.go`. Main had moved 94 commits ahead and landed an **interactive login-URL prompt** — `loginURLInteractor`, `readLoginURLAction`, and a Bubble Tea `loginURLActionModel` — inserted immediately above `openBrowser`, while this branch had rewritten `openBrowser`'s doc comment and dropped its unused context parameter. Adjacent edits, not competing ones.

Resolution: kept main's new block verbatim, then this branch's `openBrowser`. Two details worth noting:

- The function **body** merged cleanly to `return openBrowserPlatform(browserURL)` — the ShellExecute delegation survived untouched.
- Main had also shortened the under-test comment inside the body, and git took that version. That's the right outcome, not a loss: main shortened it precisely because the old rationale ("so the caller takes the here's-the-URL fallback") no longer describes how the code works.

I used a merge rather than a rebase so your colleague's checkout of the branch doesn't get invalidated by a force-push.

## Something main changed that affects our open questions

`runBrowserLogin` now prints the login URL **unconditionally** (`login.go:350`), before any browser launch, and opening the browser is an explicit keypress with a copy-to-clipboard option:

```go
fmt.Fprintf(outW, "Logging in to %s\n\n", baseURL)
printLoginURL(outW, browserLoginURLLabel, authURL)
```

So the hardening I'd been recommending landed on main independently — that decision is off the table. It also means the specific dead end your reporter hit is already gone on main: they'd now see the full URL and could copy it even with the truncating launcher. The ShellExecute fix still matters, because pressing Enter should open a URL that works.

Verified on the merged tree: builds for darwin/windows/linux, Windows test binary compiles, `mise run lint` clean plus a `GOOS=windows` pass, and `mise run test:ci` green. Net diff versus main is still exactly our 7 files (+210/−30) — the merge pulled in no collateral.

One thing that tripped me up in case you hit it: `mise run lint` fails mid-merge with *"go module files modified, please commit result of go mod tidy"*. That's a false positive — `lint:gomod` uses `git status --porcelain`, which also reports staged changes, and the merge legitimately stages main's `go.mod`. `go mod tidy` had made no changes of its own; it passes once the merge is committed.

The `/dev/tty`-on-Windows question is still open and still worth settling — say the word and I'll put up that CI probe.
